title.#text: FeN@C nanomaterials: Synergistic PTT/CDT/NO for the dynamic therapy of diabetic foot ulcer.

papers.abstract: Diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) is one of the most severe complications of diabetes, and its multiple pathological factors render treatment more challenging. We synthesized FeN@C nanomaterials to integrate synergistic photothermal therapy/chemical dynamic therapy/nitric oxide (PTT/CDT/NO) for DFU therapy. First, FeOand urea were used as precursors to synthesize FeN@C nanomaterials via nitridation. The nanomaterial can serve as a new NO donor that releases NO triggered by Hand reactive oxygen species (HOand O). Furthermore, FeN@C possess superhigh peroxidase (POD)-like activity (V = 21.1 Ms., pH 5.5), catalyzing endogenous HOinto hydroxyl radicals (OH). POD activity can also amplify NO and peroxynitrite (ONOO) production. In addition, Fe₂N@C nanomaterials reveal high near-infrared II (NIR-II) light harvest and photothermal conversion efficiency (43.94%). Hyperthermia also synergistically boosts POD-like activity and NO release. Under NIR-II laser irradiation, the combination of PTT/CDT and high NO concentration of can quickly clear bacterial infection. In addition, NO can down-regulate the expression of heat shock proteins (HSPs) to amplify PTT performance. Then, the mild NO supply (without irradiation) further facilitates the reversal of inflammation (M2 macrophage polarization) and tissue regeneration (angiogenesis). This dynamic synergistic therapy promotes fast normal DFU healing.

papers.title: PXDN knockdown alleviates hepatic stellate cell activation by regulating GPX1.
papers.journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Molecular basis of disease
papers.abstract: The central mechanism of cholestatic liver fibrosis (CLF) is the accumulation of extracellular matrix caused by the activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), which is reversible in the early to mid-stages. Therefore, this study characterized the underlying molecular mechanisms involved. In this study, the liver and spleen indexes of the CLF model markedly increased and continued to rise over time. There were significant differences in ALP, TBIL, AST, DBIL, ALT, IBIL, AST/ALT, and GGT levels among rats in the CLF and SHAM groups at different time points. Histological staining revealed that the CLF had progressed to cirrhosis by week 5. Importantly, relative to the SHAM group, the CLF-2, CLF-3, CLF-4, and CLF-5 groups contained 2886, 3472, 5297, and 4586 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), respectively. The four comparisons identified 1848 shared DEGs that regulate cell growth, chemotaxis, inflammation, apoptosis, and fibrosis. Pxdn and Gpx1 are the hub genes for these shared DEGs. Pxdn knockdown reversed the TGF-β-induced increase in HSC activity and markers (Col I, α-SMA, and FN), an effect that was rescued by Gpx1 knockdown. Pxdn knockdown increased GPX1 levels in HSCs, whereas Gpx1 knockdown had no effect on PXDN. In conclusion, Pxdn knockdown attenuated TGF-β-induced activation of HSC by upregulating GPX1. These findings nominate the PXDN-GPX1 axis as a mechanistic candidate warranting in vivo interrogation.

papers.title: Hematopoietic stem cell fitness mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are important for human health and clinical therapy. A heterogeneous pool of HSCs sustain blood production through life by balancing self-renewal and multilineage differentiation. Aging is associated with a decline in the function of the HSC pool and hematopoietic perturbations. Additionally, aging correlates with clonal hematopoiesis, driven by the accumulation of genetic mutations in this long-lived cell population that can lead to altered cell function and ultimately to leukemic transformation. Alongside their natural role in sustaining hematopoiesis, healthy HSCs are also used clinically for their regenerative capacity in stem cell transplantation, in which they reconstitute the entire adult blood system and can cure a range of blood disorders. Within these contexts, the term fitness is regularly used but often poorly defined. In this perspective, we summarize two distinct types of HSC fitness, clonal fitness and stem cell fitness. We then introduce mechanisms known to shape each and discuss the therapeutic implications for modulating HSC fitness mechanisms.

papers.title: Midbody inheritance predicts re-entry into quiescence, but not lineage potential, in mouse hematopoietic stem cells.
papers.abstract: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) self-renew and generate all blood cell lineages. During cytokinesis, the midbody is asymmetrically inherited by one daughter cell or symmetrically released, but whether these patterns affect HSC fate remains unclear. We developed a fusion protein of humanized monomeric Kusabira-Orange 2 (hmKO2) and MgcRacGAP to trace midbody inheritance and daughter-cell fate by time-lapse imaging. Using this system, we found that midbody release was associated with delayed progression to the next division but not with HSC lineage potential, suggesting that the midbody remnant may regulate cell-cycle progression.
